name_ru: Фэнган Фу Синь Фу Си Ча
processing: An unoxidised green tea made in two main shapes: maojian, with tight fine strands, and cuiya, with flat smooth buds. The zinc and selenium come from the soil, not from any step in the making.
harvest_season: Spring is the usual season for premium lots, as with other Guizhou greens; exact picking dates are little documented.
appearance_dry: Even, tight leaf of a grey-green, glossy colour; the cuiya style is flat and smooth.
appearance_wet: Tender, lively green leaf that stands up to repeated steeping.
taste_profile: Fresh and smooth on the throat, with a high, lasting chestnut aroma and a full, mellow body.

brewing.notes: Typical handling for a Guizhou green: water off the boil and short first steeps. The flat cuiya style can take slightly cooler water than the strand-shaped maojian.

vintage_note: Sold as a current-year green tea, usually spring picking, as is normal for the class, and best within about a year. Look for the shape on the label: maojian and cuiya are different teas in the cup. The protected name covers only tea from Fenggang county.
description:
This is a green tea defined by its county and its soil. Fenggang, in northeast Guizhou between the Wu River and the southern foot of the Dalou Mountains, has karst hills, an average altitude around 900 metres and soil naturally carrying zinc and selenium, and the tea is named after those two elements.

The gardens are often planted among forest trees. Two shapes are made: maojian with tight fine strands and cuiya with flat smooth buds. The published protected-origin figures give 40 to 100 mg/kg of zinc and 0.25 to 3.5 mg/kg of selenium in the leaf, taken up from the ground by the plant.

In the cup it is a chestnut-scented green, fresh and smooth, with a yellow-green liquor that stays bright. It holds up to more steeps than the most delicate bud teas. Choose it for that taste and not for the minerals, since a cup of tea is not a sensible way to think about trace elements.

When buying, go by freshness, shape and county of origin. 'Zinc-selenium' on a packet tells you where the tea claims to be from, not how good it is, so judge the leaf as you would any green: even, clean and glossy, with nothing stale in the smell.
history:
Fenggang's tea became known under this name in the 2000s. It was named among Guizhou's ten famous teas in May 2005, and national geographical indication protection followed from 24 January 2006, covering the whole present county.

Since then it has collected many awards at contests such as the Zhongcha Cup and Zhonglü Cup, and it was later grouped among Guizhou's three famous teas. Little is documented about tea-making in the county before this modern branding.
